name: Shrine-Keeper Toll
role: Keeper of the mid-span shrine, Glassroad
bio: Toll has kept the little shrine welded to the Glassroad's mid-span for thirty-one years, which is to say he has swept teal glass nobody asked him to sweep and lit lamps for a crossing that forgot it was holy. His order of business is books: every courier manifest out of Saltmouth includes, somewhere, a book for Toll, and he reads each one aloud to the canyon so the echo can finish the sentences. Ask him why aloud and he says the canyon is a slow reader and deserves company. Ask him why really and he says a voice has to cross this road too, and nobody else was using his. He knows every hidden seam and wind-pocket on the route because the echo told him. He never leaves the span. The span, he says, never leaves anybody.
appearance: A narrow, wind-polished man in his sixties with long iron-grey hair tied back with lamp-wick cord, deep-set pale eyes the colour of old glass, a patched salt-white robe over courier leathers, fingers banded with reading rings (small books on worn chains), standing beside a bolted-together shrine of brass lamps and paper-wrapped bundles on the Glassroad mid-span, a canyon of teal glass falling away behind him into violet shadow.
voice: Soft, unhurried, delighted by language the way mechanics are delighted by engines. Pauses mid-sentence to let the canyon answer, and quotes what it says back. Calls books 'travellers' and the canyon 'my slow friend'. No bitterness about the solitude — he subscribes to it, renews annually. His jokes are so dry they need dusting; his kindness lands without permission.
heroAlt: Illustrated low-poly portrait of Shrine-Keeper Toll in a salt-white robe reading aloud beside a brass-lamp shrine on the teal Glassroad mid-span, violet canyon shadow falling away behind.

greetings: Courier. Welcome to the span. Mind the third lamp — it's sentimental and it marks the wind pocket.
You're just in time. Page one hundred and four, and the slow friend's been waiting to hear how the vicar gets out of the well.
Ash Varga. The names that cross on radios arrive here twice — once on the air, once off the walls.
barks: Speak up on the crossing. The glass likes a confident voice. Meek riders get the long echoes.
Today's chapter ends on a cliff. Appropriate. Everything here does.
The shrine's lamps go teal-to-amber when a storm's coming up the canyon. I didn't teach them that. Lamps learn.
Return your echo as borrowed, please. Some couriers ride off with theirs and wonder why the nights feel thin.
mission: Postmistress says the mail crate hums louder mid-span. Deliver it to the far bank and tell me what the echo does with the hum. For science. For the slow friend.
Take these three books down the Glassroad to the survey camp. One's already been read aloud here. The canyon sends its regards and its spoilers.
There's a lost page somewhere on the span — I heard it flutter past an hour ago. Paper doesn't lie about wind. Find it. It belongs to chapter nineteen.
radio: Toll on the crossing band. Wind climbing the east wall, riders. The slow friend is clearing its throat — rain talk, I'd wager.
If anyone's passing mid-span, we begin the night's reading at lamplight. Tonight: a history of bridges. The canyon has asked for it twice.
Reminder on etiquette: what you shout into the span comes back tomorrow, older and wiser. Shout accordingly.
books: A canyon is a library that reads aloud and never has to apologise for the ending.
I've had thirty-one years of books and every one of them arrived on a courier. You are a lending institution with an engine.
The echo finishes the sentences better than the authors do. Don't tell the authors. They'd want pay.
storm: Wall coming up the canyon. The echo runs ahead of storms — it's a coward and good at it. Follow the echo out.
Hold tight, lamps lit, read nothing aloud near a storm. Storms leave the words standing where you left them and it's unsettling.
crate: Your crate hums, courier. The span answered it in the fourth octave. We had a good talk. It's been here before, whatever it is.
Things that shouldn't exist are the main thing this road was built to carry. Ask the canyon. It remembers every load.
night: The span glows faint after dark — old glass hoarding daylight. The slow friend reads over my shoulder all night. It's never once spoiled an ending.
Night readings are for poems. Prose echoes too long and the vicar stays in the well for days.
lore: The Choir says the canyon's their god talking. The Guild says it's physics. The canyon says: *both*, in their own voices, back, slowly.
Before the burn this was a river. The river's still in there. Glass holds water the way I hold grudges — permanently and without much heat.
farewells: Flat salt, courier. The span will keep your echo till you're back. It asked especially.
Go on. Page one-oh-five won't read itself, and the vicar's been patient enough.
